The height of the colored bars shows the median bill savings for the given utility and tariff scenario, while the error bars show the range of results excluding the top and bottom 10% From these load impacts, we can quantify the technical potential of price response via several different metrics. Figure ES-5 shows two of these metrics, with the total effective shed demand response shown on the top row, and aggregate customer bill savings on the bottom. The total potential shed DR is substantial, reaching 5.6 GW in 2030 across the six end uses modeled in this study. (Note that this is the weighted average load reduction across several system peak hours, as opposed to the single-hour peak reduction of over 8 GW discussed above). These six end uses account for approximately 40% of the demand that occurs in the net peak load hour; while other end uses are not expected to be quite as flexible as those targeted in this study, this viii implies that even more potential is available from response to dynamic prices. Technical potential considers universal enrollment in the dynamic tariff, adoption of load flexibility technologies, and enablement of price response capabilities. In the report, we discuss potential adoption rates of price response and how much potential can be captured by various subsets of customers. The bottom row of Figure ES-5 highlights the stark differences across the tariff design scenarios studied. While the effective shed is quite similar across tariff designs, the customer bill savings potential is dramatically reduced in the Mild tariff as compared to the Full tariff. EVs are the largest driver of potential bill savings, with space cooling coming in second. Ag crop and pool pumping loads are also significant, as their ability to save customers money year-round adds up. Savings from flexing residential water heating loads are also noticeable, and in aggregate are on par with commercial space cooling savings. Figure ES-5. Technical potential of response to dynamic prices as measured by effective shed (top) and aggregate customer bill savings (bottom) The key question regarding bill savings is whether they are sufficient to warrant investment in load flexibility technologies needed to respond to hourly prices. Figure ES-6 shows the distribution of cost-benefit ratio across all customer clusters, for each sector and end use combination and each tariff design. These results are for the lower of our two 2030 price ix forecasts; if prices are higher, the bill savings from load response will also be higher, and the cost-benefit ratios will decrease. Technology costs are modeled using past assumptions for demand response enabling technologies, as there are not generally products on the market that are currently able to respond to hourly price signals.
